Take the two setups from the top. The first has b = 0.25, so it breaks even at 1 ÷ 1.25, or 80 per cent, and it wins 70 per cent of the time: E = 0.70 × 0.25 − 0.30 = −0.125R a trade. The second has b = 5, so it breaks even at 1 ÷ 6, or 16.7 per cent, and it wins 40 per cent: E = 0.40 × 5 − 0.60 = +1.40R a trade. Seventy per cent was not enough and forty per cent was more than twice what was needed.

The middle row is worth pausing on, because you have seen both of its numbers before. At b = 1 with no costs the breakeven is 50 per cent, which is the base lesson 10 started from before it added its charges; at b = 1 with s = 0.17 it is 58.5 per cent, which is exactly the figure lesson 16 arrived at from the other direction. Three lessons, one formula, and the agreement is not a coincidence — the earlier two were this one with b fixed at 1.
